interactions.label: Which combination of clinical features in the female partner points toward andro

params.question: Which combination of clinical features in the female partner points toward androgen excess?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dysmenorrhoea with heavy bleeding suggests endometriosis or fibroids — these are not features of androgen excess.
Correct. Infrequent cycles (intervals of 45–60 days) combined with increasing facial hair are hallmark features of excess androgen production, most commonly seen in polycystic ovary syndrome.
This combination suggests hyperprolactinaemia, not androgen excess.
Regular cycles with painful intercourse point toward endometriosis, not an androgenic disorder.

overallFeedback.feedback: Oligomenorrhoea (cycles every 45–60 days) and progressive hirsutism (increasing facial hair) are classic signs of androgen excess, pointing toward PCOS as the likely underlying diagnosis.
Oligomenorrhoea with hirsutism are classic androgenic features — the most common cause in reproductive-age women is PCOS, which is also the leading cause of anovulatory infertility.

interactions.label: A single abnormal semen analysis is sufficient to confirm male factor infertilit

params.question: A single abnormal semen analysis is sufficient to confirm male factor infertility.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: A single abnormal result is not sufficient. Semen quality varies day to day due to biological factors such as recent fever, medications, and stress. Two samples spaced two to seven weeks apart are needed to confirm a persistent abnormality.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — semen parameters fluctuate with illness, stress, abstinence interval, and other factors. The WHO standard requires two samples taken two to seven weeks apart to confirm that an abnormality is persistent, not transient.

params.question: On hysterosalpingography, contrast fails to enter the right fallopian tube at the cornual junction. Which finding would best help distinguish a true proximal block from tubal spasm?

answers.text: Presence of a normal triangular uterine cavity shadow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A triangular uterine cavity is a normal HSG finding and provides no information about whether a proximal filling defect is due to true obstruction or spasm.

answers.text: Free contrast spill from the contralateral tube

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Normal spill from the opposite tube confirms its patency but tells you nothing about why the ipsilateral tube did not fill.

answers.text: Resolution of the apparent block after administering an antispasmodic agent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Approximately 15% of apparent proximal blocks on HSG are false positives caused by muscular spasm. If the block resolves after antispasmodic medication, the tube is patent and the initial finding was spasm, not true obstruction.

answers.text: A dilated, rounded appearance of the tube beyond the block

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A dilated, rounded tube is the hallmark of a hydrosalpinx — this is a distal block pattern, not a proximal one, and would not be seen if contrast cannot enter the tube at the cornu.

overallFeedback.feedback: When contrast fails to enter a tube at the cornu, the finding may be true obstruction or simple muscular spasm. Administering an antispasmodic and repeating the injection can resolve spasm-related false positives, which occur in roughly 15% of cases.

Tubal spasm at the cornu mimics true proximal obstruction in about 15% of cases. Antispasmodic challenge or laparoscopic confirmation prevents a false-positive diagnosis that could lead to unnecessary surgery.

interactions.label: What is the underlying mechanism that causes ascites, pleural effusion, and haem

params.question: What is the underlying mechanism that causes ascites, pleural effusion, and haemoconcentration in ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome?

answers.text: Excessive oestrogen causes direct renal sodium and water retention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although oestrogen levels are elevated in OHSS, the fluid shifts result from vascular leak, not from primary renal sodium retention.

answers.text: Gonadotrophins directly damage the peritoneal mesothelium, causing transudation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Gonadotrophins act on ovarian follicles, not on the peritoneal lining. The fluid leak is a systemic vascular phenomenon, not local peritoneal damage.

answers.text: Hyperstimulated ovaries release VEGF, which increases capillary permeability and shifts protein-rich fluid into extravascular spaces

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. VEGF from overstimulated ovaries makes capillaries throughout the body leaky. Protein-rich fluid escapes into the peritoneum and pleural cavity, while the remaining intravascular blood becomes concentrated, raising the risk of thromboembolism.

answers.text: Rupture of multiple follicles releases blood into the peritoneal cavity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While follicular rupture can cause minor bleeding, the hallmark fluid accumulation in OHSS is a protein-rich transudate driven by capillary leak, not haemoperitoneum from ruptured follicles.

overallFeedback.feedback: In OHSS, hyperstimulated ovaries release large amounts of VEGF, making capillaries leaky throughout the body. Protein-rich fluid shifts into extravascular spaces, causing ascites and pleural effusion while concentrating the blood and raising the risk of life-threatening thrombosis.

VEGF-driven capillary permeability is the central mechanism of OHSS. This single pathway explains every downstream complication — ascites, pleural effusion, haemoconcentration, oliguria, and thromboembolism.

params.question: A 43-year-old woman is told that IVF has a 'forty percent success rate.' Why is this statement clinically misleading?

answers.text: Because IVF success is measured per embryo transferred, not per cycle started

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Success rates are typically reported per cycle, not per embryo. The real problem with the quoted figure is the absence of age stratification.

answers.text: Because the 40% figure applies to women under 35; at age 43, her live birth rate with her own oocytes may be as low as 2–5%

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. IVF success depends primarily on oocyte quality, which declines steeply with age. Quoting an overall average without specifying age gives a 43-year-old a falsely optimistic picture and may lead to costly, emotionally draining cycles with very little realistic chance of a live birth.

answers.text: Because the statistic includes only clinical pregnancies, not live births

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While the distinction between clinical pregnancy and live birth rates matters, the primary source of misinformation here is the failure to stratify by the patient's age.

answers.text: Because IVF success depends on sperm quality, which has not been assessed in this patient's partner

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although male factor affects outcomes, female age — specifically oocyte quality — is the single strongest predictor of IVF success. The misleading element is the unqualified average, not incomplete male assessment.

overallFeedback.feedback: IVF live birth rates decline steeply with age — from around 40% under 35 to as low as 2–5% in the mid-forties. Quoting the overall average without age stratification is misleading and may drive older patients into repeated, futile cycles.

Female age is the dominant predictor of IVF success. Live birth rates fall from ~40% under 35 to single digits by the mid-forties. Honest counselling must present age-specific rates so patients can make informed decisions.
